en: The Seventh [Chapter]: Contemplating the Objects of Various Views, as spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty and recorded by his disciple Guanding.
"Various" means not one; false interpretations are termed "views. Furthermore, [it continues:]
To understand and know this is the meaning of "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
When one infers incorrectly and yet forms a clear, decisive understanding through a biased perspective,
it is termed a "view."

Now, those who listen to students reciting names and characteristics and form interpretations based solely on the literal text have not yet opened their mental eyes; they possess no rational contemplation whatsoever.
Those who rely on the text are born, but those who lack realization die.
Now, those who practice meditation value only rational contemplation (*yuan-guan*), such that their minds are harmonized with everything they encounter;
yet they remain ignorant of names and signs (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), not recognizing a single phrase.
Those who recite the texts cling to the stump, while those whose emotions are attuned achieve wondrous awakening.
If both schools omit critical discussion, they both fail.
If one’s insight is unimpeded and one is conversant with terminology,
then when questioned by others regarding that insight, one’s meaning will be inexhaustible.
It is like a bird flying in circles after being shot from a curved bow, losing its way;
yet when explaining difficult questions, one possesses ample skill,
like an arrow shot into the vast void that travels without obstruction.
One should know that this is not accomplished through study, but must be produced by insight (*darśana*).
This insight may arise either from meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) or from hearing (*śruta*).
For example, when the untainted (*anāsrava*) arises, it relies upon faith, the Dharma, and hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī* wisdom).
Regarding those who develop [faith] through hearing: although they did not originally listen extensively or in great detail, they are able to transform their understanding and awaken;
their views and insights are clear, and they are sharp-witted in debate and response.
Regarding those who attain realization through meditation:
initially, because the mind is tranquil, subsequent contemplation becomes increasingly clear;
as one turns and transforms with mastery, it is as if there were a wondrous penetration.
In the south, those who practice meditation are few, and those who manifest [realization] are rare;
in the north, such occurrences are many.
People remain blind and ignorant, yet they claim to have attained the true Way or to have attained dhāraṇī.
Those who are ignorant in discerning people regard this high and secure state as either something not to be believed or as a delusion;
thus it is now said that it is neither madness nor sainthood.
Generally, when a ghost possesses someone, they can speak; once the ghost departs, the person becomes mute and deluded.
Since this is not the case here, we know it is not madness.
Upon examining the cause, one finds that the delusions of greed and hatred still persist.
Based on these new delusions, afflictions increase further;
the fetters of the eighty-eight *anuśayas* become vast and pervasive.
Thus, one knows that this is not the state of a sage, but merely the arousal of views and wisdom.
In general discussion, [insight] arises through the causes of hearing, learning, and meditation, but it occurs most frequently through meditation.
Sometimes insight arises after meditation has already been attained; sometimes meditation and insight arise together.
Furthermore, once insight has been attained, one may subsequently attain meditation; moreover, when both meanings are present, the latter case is more common.
For example, while various dhyānas can all give rise to the outflow-free (anāsrava),
those that have actually given rise to it are few;
in the six stages and the nine stages, however, those that give rise to it are many.
For this reason, following the discussion of the objects of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the various views (*dṛṣṭi*) are now addressed.
If a person possesses sharp and keen faculties and is capable of self-correction,
or if they seek out the sūtras and śāstras to examine their own faults;
Such a person is difficult to find.
If one cannot rectify oneself,
one must encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who clearly demonstrates right and wrong to shatter one's biased views.
This, too, is difficult to encounter.
Therefore, it is said that the true Dharma, as well as the teacher and the audience who listen to it, are difficult to find.
Thus, one neither awakens by oneself nor encounters a teacher.
The sun of heterodoxy increases daily, while the moon of birth and death wanes ever more severely.
Like dragging a crooked log through a dense forest, how can one expect to reach the end?
Now, observe that the objects of various views are categorized into four.
First, the explanation of the persons who hold various views;
second, the explanation of the causes and conditions that give rise to these views;
third, the explanation of their faults.
The fourth section clarifies *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Regarding the first [point], clarifying the various views concerning persons and dharmas, there are further two parts.
The first concerns the differences among those with false views.
Second, there are differences in the adherence to false teachings by those of wrong views.
Those of wrong views are further divided into three categories.
The first consists of non-Buddhists who stand outside the Buddha-dharma.
Second, those who are attached to non-Buddhist paths while within the Buddha-dharma;
third, those who study the Buddha-dharma but become non-Buddhists.
First, external non-Buddhists.
There are three fundamental sources.
The first is the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) Kapila— translated here as "Yellow-Headed"—
who maintains that the effect exists within the cause.
Second is Āulūkya, translated here as Xiuhou (Ulūka),
who maintains that the effect does not exist within the cause.
Third is Lèshāpó (Lokāyata), translated here as Kuxing (Asceticism).
It is reckoned that within the cause there is both fruit and no fruit.
Furthermore, the *Mahāyānāvatāra-śāstra* states:
"In the teachings of Kapila, there is the error of reckoning [cause and effect] as identical."
The agent and the action are one;
the characteristic and that which possesses the characteristic are one; the part and the whole are one.
Those such as these are called those who reckon [the self and the world] as one.
The Ulūka-sāṃkhyas reckon them as different;
the Kālakauṭas reckon them as both one and different.
If the son of Tika reckons them as neither identical nor different,
while all the non-Buddhists and Makkhali and others reckon them as different,
none of these views deviate from these four positions.
From the three or four non-Buddhist schools, branches and streams branched out;
by the time the Buddha appeared, there were six great masters, namely Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa is his clan name.
He maintains that there is neither birth nor extinction.
Makkhali Gosāla maintains that the suffering and pleasure of sentient beings have no causes or conditions and occur spontaneously.
Saṃjayin Vairaṭīputra reckoned that sentient beings attain the Way when their time has matured after eighty thousand kalpas;
he held that this is reached when the counting of thread-balls reaches its limit. Ajita Keśakambalin—
*Kambala* refers to coarse cloth.
Calculating the suffering of karmic retribution, he would rather substitute it with such acts as throwing oneself from a cliff or plucking out one's hair.
Kāṛyāyaṇa Kātyāyana calculates that things both exist and do not exist.
"Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta maintains that what is produced by karma is fixed and absolutely cannot be changed.
This is from Kumārajīva’s commentary;
its name is the same as in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, and its tenets consist of three points of agreement and three points of difference.
Perhaps there are errors in the translation, or perhaps there is another underlying meaning;
these matters remain undetermined at present.
However, in its general substance, it inherits the tradition of Kapila and others.
Based on the root [text], there are three;
alternatively, there may be four, namely the four views.
The second, those who adhere to the Buddha-dharma while following external paths, originated with the Vātsīputrīyas.
Vaipulya [sutras] arose because those who were naturally intelligent read the Buddha’s scriptures and developed a singular insight;
they were given this name because they were associated with the emergence of the Buddha-dharma.
The Vātsīputrīya, reading the *Śāriputrābhidharma*, formulated his own distinct interpretation, saying:
"I exist within the fifth, the inexpressible treasury (*avaktavyakośa*), outside of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
What are the four propositions?"
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reckon that form is the self,
that there is a self apart from form,
or that the self exists within form.
"I have form within myself.
The four aggregates are likewise.
Combined, these constitute twenty types of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"To destroy the twenty types of *satkāya-dṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) and thereby become a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer)" refers precisely to this meaning.
Now, the Vātsīputrīyas maintain that the self (*ātman*) is distinct from the six teachers.
Furthermore, if one rejects all treatises that do not accord with the Buddha-dharma,
this constitutes the "dharma of heterodox persons" attached to the Buddha-dharma.
Or it is said:
The three periods of time and unconditioned phenomena constitute the four propositions.
Furthermore, the practitioners of the Vaipulya school, relying on their own cleverness, read the Buddha’s ten similes and formulated their own interpretation, saying:
"Non-arising and non-ceasing, like an illusion or a transformation, with illusory emptiness as its tenet.
Nāgārjuna rejected this, saying:
"This is not the Buddha-dharma; it is the work of the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna]."
This is also the dharma of heterodox persons.
By studying the Buddha-dharma in three ways, one becomes a follower of external paths;
clinging to the gates of the Buddhist teachings, one gives rise to afflictions and fails to enter the principle.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"If one enters the Abhidharma without the skillful means of Prajñā,
one falls into existence."
Entering emptiness leads to falling into the extreme of non-existence;
entering *kun-lê* (the universal) leads to falling into the extreme of both existence and non-existence.
As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
To cling to the notion that things are neither existent nor non-existent is called the doctrine of delusion;
it is to perversely grasp the True Dharma and thereby become a follower of false teachings.
If one studies the four gates of the Mahāyāna in such a manner, one immediately loses the true intent of Prajñā.
Because those burned by the fire of false views revert to becoming followers of heterodox dharmas,
the *Śata-śāstra* correctly refutes external non-Buddhists;

now, the Mahāyāna masters fiercely refute the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, asserting that they are non-Buddhists who cling to the extremes of existence and non-existence.
However, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"Among the three baskets, it is the emptiness of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
This, however, seems to be intended in the sense of non-existence.
Furthermore, it treats the views of a hundred schools as correct and those of a hundred schools as incorrect.
Its shifting interpretations of the meaning resemble the notion that the effect exists within the cause and yet does not exist within the cause;
it also resembles the intent of the *Kun-le* (Abhidharma).
In that age, when discussions arose, everyone attained the Way.
In this age, those who cling to [fixed views] are the ones who have lost it; how does this concern the fault of the Dharma?
This matter should be treated with composure and must not be equated with the views of Kapila and others.
If one were to argue that the "great" refutes the "small"— as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* critiques—
then by failing to perceive the Middle Way, such a position would be identical to that of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
This is not intended to deprive them of their skillful means.
Second, regarding the clarification that those who hold to heterodox views differ in their adherence to the Dharma, the *Guāngzhōng Shù* states:
"Each master possesses three kinds of Dharma."
First, attaining the dharma of omniscience;
second, attaining the dharma of supernormal powers;
third, attaining the dharma of the Vedas.
All those who possess omniscience each give rise to a single kind of view based on their respective calculations;
with minds of clear and sharp understanding, they extend this view and wisdom to encompass all phenomena.
Therefore, they are called the "Non-Buddhists of All-Knowledge.
As for those with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*),
having attained the five *abhijñās*, they can transform cities into salt marshes.
They transform humans into sheep,
stop rivers with their ears, and reach out to touch the sun and moon;
these are called the non-Buddhist practitioners of supernatural powers (ṛddhi).
As for the Vedic dharma,
those who are able to understand and know all worldly scripts, astrology, medicine, military arts,
and commerce are called outsiders of the Vedas.
There are three different ways in which a single teacher may attain the Dharma.
The Vātsīputrīyas and the Vaipulya school are likewise.
If one examines their adherence to the Buddha’s teachings according to the heterodox interpretations of the Three Piṭakas and the four gates:
There are three aspects to this single gate:
first, the direct arousal of the nature of understanding and liberating wisdom, which gives rise to vision;
second, the attainment of the various supernormal powers.
One understands the words and letters of the four Āgamas through these three methods.
Thus, within these four gates, there are twelve different ways of attaining the Dharma.
If one grasps the essential meaning, [one transcends these].
Within each gateway, there are initially three kinds of foundations of mindfulness:
first, the foundation of mindfulness of intrinsic nature; second, the shared foundation of mindfulness.
The three applications of mindfulness have as their nature the direct contemplation of the principles of the truths;
together, they constitute the combined cultivation of both phenomena and principles.
This condition is a universal condition for all objects;
it is also a condition for the teachings of the Tripiṭaka.
Later, at the time of realizing the fruit, three kinds of liberation are accomplished.
There are those liberated through wisdom, those liberated through both [wisdom and concentration], and those liberated without doubt.
Therefore, when the Dharma-piṭaka was compiled, one thousand people were selected;
all of them were liberated without doubt and had thoroughly mastered both internal and external scriptures.
Regarding the subduing of external enemies,
the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Liberation from the hindrance of afflictions and liberation from the hindrance to meditative concentration."
Those who have attained liberation through wisdom by being freed from the obstacles to all phenomena attain the first liberation.
Those who have attained common liberation attain the second liberation.
Only a Buddha attains the third liberation.
This is collectively termed "liberation through the resolution of doubt.
Regarding those who lose their way regarding the four gates— Shared, Distinct, and Complete— of the Mahāyāna,
there are likewise thirty-six types of differing ways of attaining the Dharma.
The second section, explaining the arousal of various views, has two parts:
first, explaining the arousal of various views;
second, the differences in the arousal of views.
First, regarding those who manifest through clear vision:
it may be due to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) or due to hearing [the teachings].
Throughout kalpas of long duration, there is nothing that sentient beings have not done.
Having previously practiced various views, one forgets them during the interval between lifetimes;
because of the concealment of transgressions, the original understanding does not quickly open.
Now, if the obstructions are thin, one can give rise to the various dhyānas.
Sometimes insight arises simultaneously with meditative concentration, or it arises after concentration has ceased;
sometimes insight is born suddenly upon hearing another's explanation.
It is like a spring of water obstructed by earth and stone.
Once the obstructions and stagnations are cleared away, it flows forth as a river.
When the dark veils are removed and the weeds of discrimination are swept away,
day after day and for ten days, it continues on and on without ceasing.
Each instance of attachment is itself difficult to overcome, yet each instance of attachment is itself liberated.
Where there is grasping, there is substantiality, yet there is penetration;
where there is no grasping, there is emptiness, yet it dissolves of its own accord.
Furthermore, eloquence is unimpeded, skillfully explaining one's own Dharma and adorning one's speech;
when others come to challenge with difficult questions, one is exquisitely able to provide explanations and resolutions. From where does such insight arise?
Within dhyāna, there is the factor of insight (vipaśyanā).
Insight is a mental factor of wisdom (prajñā).
If one observes all phenomena with negligence, one will not know when to stop.
A swift horse covered in sweat cannot be controlled.

Likewise, if those who listen to the teachings lack the moisture of *dhyāna*, they will attempt to engage in conceptual discrimination at the very outset; their intestines will be pulled out and they will vomit blood.
Consequently, they will lose their lives before the vision of the ultimate truth is achieved.
If the power of concentration moistens the insight, then even if it is lax and difficult to control,
one will not reach the point of "pulling out the entrails" [of distraction], but will instead achieve much realization.
From this branch of insight, one proceeds to investigate and analyze the principles.
This refers to the view that the effect exists within the cause among all phenomena.
This interpretation is clear and sharp, penetratingly seeing the profound intent and surpassing other people;
when used to challenge others, they are unable to understand it.
That is to say, although others speak falsely,
one clings to one's own position such that others cannot refute it,
and one considers it to be true.
The sublime mind that attains the principle of non-arising true wisdom—if one examines it closely—is merely the mundane knowledge and eloquence of view-delusions;
it is fully possessed by the net of inverted delusions consisting of the eighty-eight *anuśayas*. How could it have anything to do with true understanding?
One should know that this is the manifestation of the view of Kapila.
Furthermore, by investigating the factors of meditation (*dhyānāṅga*), one seeks out how there is no effect within the cause among all phenomena;
this view is distinct and the understanding of the mind is sharp and intense.
Although they may raise various objections and employ various refutations,
citing various proofs to establish that the effect does not exist within the cause,
these cannot withstand the critique of this [position].
Anything else is false speech.
When another comes to refute one's own position, that very refutation is grasped and transformed into what is held to be true.
To propose that the ultimate goal consists solely in the absence of an effect within the cause should be understood as being definitively inspired by the Sāṃkhya view. If, however,
one contemplates the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) while reflecting on how an effect both exists and does not exist within the cause, [that is correct].
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Existence contends with non-existence;
non-existence contends with existence."
To say that Dīrghanakha maintains both existence and non-existence and disputes with those who hold to existence or non-existence—
if one enters this view, the questioning would be endless;
is this not the arising of the Laisavāda view?
The calculations of those six teachers differ;
one must skillfully grasp the intent of each teacher's position so as to verify it against their expressed views.

This refers to the manifestation of the views of the six teachers.

rather, it resides within the fifth, the Ineffable Treasury.
When this view is awakened, the mind becomes clear and sharp, capable of both questioning and answering.
Divine and swift, he is difficult to withstand in combat;

Viewing it as a whole, one perceives impermanence and non-self;
yet, reckoning this as real,
the resulting views are entirely consistent with the Abhidharma.
Although the veteran listeners understood the terminology and definitions, their mental pathways remained obstructed;
yet if they were to give rise to this insight, even if it were obscure in its textual expression, their spiritual understanding would be a hundredfold greater.
Those who do not recognize this mistake them for sages and holy ones, though they are not.
If this is the case for a worthy person, their mind of the Path is profound and arises simultaneously with understanding;
they are able to subdue the afflictions and attain the stage of skillful means.
Yet now, although they understand impermanence, it increases their strife and contention.
The mind of the Way sinks and fades while afflictions blaze ever more fiercely;
thus one knows this is the arising of views from the gate of existence (*bhava-mukha*).
If, during the stage of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), a sudden understanding of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) arises, [it is likewise a sign of such views].
They claim that all things are impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing, and are but a collection of three provisional aggregates, empty and insubstantial;
through various skillful means, they analyze phenomena into atoms and enter into emptiness.

this is real, while all else is false.

The treatise states that when one does not transcend habitual tendencies and gives rise to non-concentration,

One should know that when the four gates accord with principle, one achieves right view;
if one loses the skillful means and falls into the four views,
it is therefore called "internal heterodoxy within the Buddha-dharma."
Not only do those who cling to the three baskets and the four gates form false views;
even those who have studied the Mahāyāna— including the Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Complete teachings— for immeasurable kalpas may fail to enter the principle,
yet they maintain their own positions as being correct.
Having been scorched by the fire of the four extreme views,
a sudden realization now dawns within the branch of contemplation:
that all existence is like flowers in the sky seen in a dream, and like an illusion.
By forming this understanding, one's discernment of the mind becomes clear and sharp;
or, by considering that illusions are fundamentally unreal and that because they are unreal they are empty,
one's understanding of emptiness becomes clear and sharp.
Alternatively, one may form the understanding that it is both empty and existent,
like a magically conjured object which is seen yet cannot be grasped. Or,
one may form the understanding that it is neither empty nor existent.
It is neither that which exists as an illusion nor that which is non-existent as an illusion.
As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, in the "Examination of Phenomena" (*Dharmaparīkṣā*), states:
"If one says that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent..."

there is nothing that cannot be dismantled among what is to be refuted, and nothing that cannot be established among what remains.

it is because true speech arises from false speech and gives rise to the view of speech.
Because Nirvana arises from craving for birth and death,
those who consume too much nectar harm their lives and die prematurely;
they lose the gateway of skillful means and fall into false attachments.
Therefore, these are called internal wrong views.
Now, the four views are the root of all views;
"self" and "other" are further the roots of the "common" and "uncaused" views.
Therefore, after Nāgārjuna has finished refuting [arising] from self and other, he points out that there are two faults in [arising] from both; moreover, arising without a cause is impossible.

The fundamental aim is to shatter the root and topple the branches;

such is the intent here. If one were to establish examples based on self, other, both, or no cause, then the biased attachments and settled views of the four gates of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna would be established.
Having thus clarified the perspectives of both ourselves and others, the remainder may be understood.
According to the Tripiṭaka, it is explained that the arising of the Great Birth and the arising of the Small Birth both proceed from ignorance and do not originate from the Truth.

The Shared Teaching clarifies that reality is non-arising;
because it is non-arising, it gives rise to all delusions.
If these delusions are extinguished, it is likewise by means of non-arising.
Such an adherence is the false view of other-nature (*parabhāva-mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Within the realm [of existence], one takes afflictions to be self and the true [nature] to be other;
therefore, this statement is made.
Outside the realm [of the specific teachings], one takes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as self and ignorance as other.

through the wisdom cultivated through conditions, this ignorance is extinguished.
To claim that arising and ceasing are unrelated to the dharma-nature (dharmatā) is a false view based on the attachment to the nature of others (parabhāva).
In the Perfect Teaching (Ekanaya), it is argued that all phenomena arise from the dharma-nature.

this is the false view of imputing an intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Previously, the ruler was weak and the ministers were powerful.

the remaining two cases can be known by analogy.
Indeed, through extensive learning one develops reasoning, while through limited study one develops supernatural powers and the Vedas.
Because of meditation (*dhyāna*), supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are frequently manifested; because of the Vedas (*veda*), insight into principle (*tattvadarśana*) is rarely manifested.
Those who manifest insight into principle subdue practitioners of the Way (*śaikṣa*);
those who manifest supernatural powers subdue worldly people.
Worldly people grasp at difference and do not grasp at understanding;
students grasp at understanding and do not grasp at difference.
The emergence of the Vedas subdues both.
Those who possess all three types of development are most capable of subduing both [the afflictions and the hindrances].
That which is developed through dhyāna has already been explained above;
that which is developed through hearing shall now be explained.
Although the practitioner has attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he has not yet awakened to the essential truth; he must rely on another person to inspire his mind.
Once his mind is tranquil and sharp, he suddenly hears that the effect exists within the cause.
The mind opened wide in awakening, clearly penetrating through erroneous wisdom;
with hundreds of thousands of layers of meaning, it became ever deeper and more profound,
like a spring in a rock.
